target.projectDescription: postgraas_server v2.0.0b1 (CHANGES.rst top entry; setup.cfg name 'postgraas_server', 'Postgraas is a super simple PostgreSQL-as-a-service', author Sebastian Neubauer, Apache-2) - a small Flask REST service (package tree ~849 lines across 18 .py files; 1610 baseline LOC in the database snapshot) that provisions PostgreSQL database instances on demand. Two flask-restful resources are registered in create_app.py at /api/v2/postgraas_instances (collection) and /api/v2/postgraas_instances/<int:id> (item). Backends are pluggable via postgraas_server/backends: a docker backend (talks to the docker daemon; no SQL) and a pg_cluster backend (postgres_cluster_driver.py, psycopg2 DB-API against a shared PostgreSQL cluster, where all SQL statements are built with str.format and executed via cursor.execute). The meta DB (DBInstance rows) is accessed through flask-sqlalchemy ORM only.

inputBoundaryInventory.summary: postgraas_server v2.0.0b1 is a small Flask REST service for PostgreSQL-as-a-service. Input boundaries: (1) the HTTP surface - two flask-restful resources registered in create_app.py:37-38; external input enters via reqparse.RequestParser().parse_args() in DBInstanceCollectionResource.post (management_resources.py:123-133: postgraas_instance_name, db_name, db_username, db_pwd, all required str) and DBInstanceResource.delete (management_resources.py:72-74: db_pwd), plus the <int:id> URL converter (int-typed) feeding the get/delete method parameters; the health/metrics routes and the plain @app.route('/health') handler take no input. No flask request.args/form/json/body/header/cookie attribute reads exist anywhere in the package. (2) the CLI surface - three console scripts (setup.cfg entry_points: postgraas_init=init_db:main, postgraas_create=backends.docker.create_db:main, prometheus_app=prometheus_app:run_server); run_server is click-decorated with --test/--port options, the two main() entry points take no arguments. (3) configuration - get_config() reads a JSON application.cfg (configuration.py:31-32) and optionally /secrets via secure-config (configuration.py:19-20); operator-level trust, not attacker input. (4) the meta DB itself - DBInstance rows read through the SQLAlchemy ORM (entity.username / entity.db_name / entity.port / entity.container_id) are re-fed into the backend delete path. The data access layer has three distinct channels: (a) the SQLAlchemy ORM (DBInstance model, DBInstance.query.get/filter_by/all, db.session.add/delete/commit - all parameterized, no raw SQL observed anywhere in the ORM usage), (b) psycopg2 DB-API in the pg_cluster backend driver (postgres_cluster_driver.py) where every statement is assembled with str.format and executed via cursor.execute with NO bound parameters, and (c) psycopg2.connect() calls (connection credential channel, not SQL text). The docker backend talks to the docker daemon API and executes no SQL.

the data-access layer is postgres_cluster_driver.py; every function parameter of that module is the SQL-layer trust boundary: _create_pg_connection(config) (:5), check_db_or_user_exists(db_name, db_user, config) (:19), create_postgres_db(connection_dict, config) (:30), get_normalized_username(username) (:56), delete_database(db_name, config) (:60), delete_user(username, config) (:70)

at the call chain, check_db_or_user_exists receives connection_dict['db_name']/['db_username'] which originate from the HTTP POST arguments; delete_database/delete_user receive entity.db_name/entity.username which originate from meta-DB rows created from HTTP POST arguments

these are intermediate propagation nodes, not external sources; emitted for labeling triage

the returned entity rows are re-used downstream: entity.username / entity.db_name / entity.port feed psycopg2.connect (:81-87) and the backend delete path -> pgcd.delete_database(entity.db_name) / pgcd.delete_user(entity.username) -> DROP DATABASE / DROP USER SQL

channelInventory.psycopg2CursorExecute: cursor.execute(query) with the SQL text at positional argument 0 - the ONLY SQL execution member observed in this project: postgres_cluster_driver.py:22, :24, :43, :44, :50, :52 (all inside the pg_cluster driver, receivers are the local `cur` from `with con.cursor() as cur`) and prometheus_app.py:40 (receiver `cursor`, static literal SQL). executemany(), executescript(), and callproc() are NOT observed anywhere and are deliberately not matched.
channelInventory.sqlalchemyOrm: flask-sqlalchemy ORM only: DBInstance.query.get/filter_by/all, db.session.add/delete/commit, db.drop_all()/create_all() in management_database.py:73-74. All parameterized; no db.engine.execute, no sqlalchemy text(), no from_statement(), no connection.cursor() raw channel observed in this snapshot - recorded as absent, no rules fabricated.
channelInventory.dynamicSqlSites: postgres_cluster_driver.py:22 ("SELECT 1 FROM pg_database WHERE datname='{}';".format(db_name)) and :24 ("SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname='{}';".format(db_user)) - .format() directly as the execute argument; :36-41 (create_role / drop_role / grant_role / create_database templates formatted with **connection_dict / keyword values into locals executed at :43/:44/:50/:52); :65 (DROP DATABASE "{}".format(db_name)); :75 (DROP USER "{}".format(get_normalized_username(username))). All 8 construction sites are .format() calls; no f-string, no '%'-interpolation, and no string-concatenation SQL construction is observed in non-test code (families kept in the query but expected to yield zero rows).
channelInventory.prometheusLiteralSql: prometheus_app.py:36-40: sql = ("SELECT count(*) FROM pg_database WHERE datistemplate = false;") then cursor.execute(sql) - a string literal, fully static; captured by the sql_text family row, not dangerous by construction
channelInventory.parameterizedSites: NO DB-API bound-parameter channel exists in this project: none of the 7 cursor.execute call sites passes a second positional argument (the bound_params family is kept in the query for cross-project contract consistency and is expected to yield zero rows). The only parameterized SQL channel is the SQLAlchemy ORM (filter_by keyword binding, session persistence).
channelInventory.connectChannel: psycopg2.connect(...) call sites (postgres_cluster_driver.py:10-16 keyword-style; management_resources.py:81-87 keyword-style with user=entity.username, password=args['db_pwd']; utils.py:12; prometheus_app.py:23-29) carry connection credentials, not SQL text - out of CWE-89 SQL-text scope, deliberately NOT emitted as sink rows (documented here).
channelInventory.dockerChannel: backends/docker/postgres_instance_driver.py talks to the docker daemon (containers.create/get/remove) - not a SQL channel, no sink rules emitted

sinkFamilies.sanitizingShapes: No input validation or quoting is applied to db_name / db_username / db_pwd before the .format() interpolation in postgres_cluster_driver.py: get_normalized_username (driver :56-57) only splits at '@' and is not a SQL sanitizer; the double-quote quoting in the GRANT template (:38) and DROP templates (:65, :75) is partial identifier quoting applied to only some of the interpolated values, and the CREATE USER/CREATE DATABASE templates (:36, :41) interpolate the raw values unquoted. The reqparse type=str coercion performs no sanitization. These facts are recorded as context for the labeling/filtering stages; sanitizer modeling is not part of this extraction round.

inputBoundaryInventory.nonVulnerabilityNote: The values interpolated into the driver's SQL templates originate from the HTTP POST/DELETE request arguments (db_name, db_username, db_pwd via db_credentials/connection_dict) and from meta-DB row fields (entity.db_name, entity.username via the delete path, which were themselves created from POST arguments) - these are candidates for the labeling step to triage, NOT presumed vulnerable in this round. The config-file and CLI input families are operator-level trust. No conclusion about any specific endpoint, file, or call being vulnerable is drawn here.

extraction.executionPlan: codeql query run (sequential, one at a time) + codeql bqrs decode --format=csv; NOT database analyze / SARIF. Execution is deferred to the next round per the task contract (generation only).
extraction.metadataForm: plain multi-column select queries carrying @name/@description/@id/@tags only; intentionally no @kind problem (wrong shape for multi-column candidate tables) and no @kind table (not assumed to exist).
columnContract: node (location-backed AST node; decodes as file:line:col)
arg_index (0-based positional argument index, -1 when not applicable; parameter rows use the 0-based position with `self` excluded)
match_kind ('api' = resolved real API call via API graphs, 'ast' = syntax-level match)

matchKindSemantics.api: call resolved through semmle.python.ApiGraphs; in this project NO source or sink row is expected to resolve at API level: the SQL execution receivers are local cursor variables from `with con.cursor() as cur` context managers, the request data arrives through flask-restful reqparse instances and framework-injected method parameters, and the backend dispatch goes through the Flask app object attribute current_app.postgraas_backend - none of these bind to library API graph nodes. The column is kept for cross-project contract consistency.
matchKindSemantics.ast: pure AST shape match (attribute/name text, syntactic receiver, decorator shapes, class-base names). The execute matching is receiver-name-agnostic (any <obj>.execute(...) matches), which tolerates cursor aliasing (cur, cursor) but cannot prove the receiver is a database cursor - name-collision noise is possible and is left to the labeling step. In non-test package code, .execute call sites occur only in the driver and prometheus_app modules.

exclusions: paths containing /tests/ (17 of the 35 .py files in the database snapshot; excluded per the workflow noise rules - the integration tests also exercise the driver SQL, but test code is filtered)
/postgraas_server-db/ and /postgraas_server-safe-db/ (the two CodeQL database directories nested inside the source tree)
extraction.expectedVolume: small project - roughly 50 source rows (parse_args 2, route_param 2, cli 2, open 2, json.load 2, api_param 11 across the 6 driver functions, wrapper_param 10 across PGClusterBackend/DockerBackend methods, internal_transfer 9 pgcd args + 4 backend-dispatch args + 6 DBInstance kwargs, db_content 4 ORM query calls) and roughly 30 sink rows (7 sql_text execute sites, 0 bound_params, 8 sql_format_call construction nodes, 5 internal_sql_wrapper functions, ~10 orm_query channel rows). f-string / percent / concat construction families are expected to yield zero rows (not observed in non-test code).

uncoveredCases: Positional-argument scan cap: the internal_transfer family enumerates argument positions 0-9 (i is bound by range membership before the indexed Call.getPositionalArg(i) lookup, because the index parameter of getPositionalArg is a checked/total-function input in QL); calls with more than 10 positional arguments would not be scanned. No such call exists in this snapshot (the widest call is create_postgres_db with 2).

Dynamic backend dispatch: current_app.postgraas_backend.create/delete/exists (management_resources.py:95/:107/:158/:164) resolve to DockerBackend or PGClusterBackend only at runtime via config['backend']['type'] and the BACKENDS dict in backends/__init__.py:4. The extraction records the call sites and both wrapper classes' parameters, but cannot prove which implementation receives the values; the pgcd.* rows capture the pg_cluster continuation only.

DBInstance(...) constructor call arguments are keyword arguments (management_resources.py:150-157); they are emitted as internal_transfer rows with arg_index -1 (keyword arguments have no positional index in the column contract; the keyword names are visible at the node location). Keyword-argument transfers into pgcd.* / backend methods are not separately enumerated - no such call site exists in this snapshot.

Chained ORM calls: DBInstance.query.filter_by(...).first() (management_resources.py:135-136) - the outer .first() call's object expression is the filter_by() call result, not an Attribute named 'query', so only the filter_by row is emitted; .first() itself is not captured as db_content/orm_query.

Dict-value propagation: the db_credentials dict literal values (management_resources.py:142-148) flow into subscript reads (connection_dict['db_name'] etc. in the driver) - only the whole dict is captured as the internal_transfer argument; per-key element flow is a dataflow/summary modeling concern for Step 4, not extraction.

Field/attribute propagation: entity.db_name / entity.username / entity.port / entity.container_id reads (management_resources.py:82-86, :97, :107, :18-19 in backends/postgres_cluster/__init__.py) and the DBInstance.__init__ self-assignments (management_resources.py:37-44) are not extracted as rows; taint through object attributes requires summary modeling in Step 4.

reqparse per-field rows: parse_args() is emitted as a single boundary row per call site; the add_argument field-name strings ('postgraas_instance_name', 'db_name', 'db_username', 'db_pwd') are string literals, not nodes, so no per-field rows are emitted - field names are visible in the source context around the row location.
flask request-object attribute reads (request.args/form/json/body/headers/cookies) do not exist in this package (flask.md cue families); no rules were fabricated for them.

psycopg2.connect keyword arguments (user/password/database/host/port) are a connection-credential channel, not SQL text; per the sink modeling decision (SQL query text or SQL-syntax-influencing fragments only) they are NOT emitted as sink rows and are recorded here instead. Same for the docker daemon API calls in backends/docker/postgres_instance_driver.py.
secure_config decryption (sec.load_secret_dict, configuration.py:36-37) returns decrypted config values through an external library; not extracted (operator-level trust, external-lib boundary).
sqlalchemy text()/from_statement()/engine.execute() and Django raw-SQL channels are absent from this snapshot; no sink rules were fabricated for them.
The safe database directory postgraas_server-safe-db inside the source tree was neither read nor traversed beyond confirming it is a database directory.
